Planner conversation toolkit · Canada and British Columbia

Explain investing clearly, and honestly.

Nine short visual conversations. Pick the client’s question, adjust the chart together, and let the talking points guide you.

  • Historical data published, dated and sourced
  • Illustration your assumptions, not a forecast
  • 2026 rules current limits and tax rates

For conversations, not promises. Investment returns and recoveries are not guaranteed, fees and risk matter, and mutual funds are not suitable for everyone.

01Inflation and cash

“Why not just keep it in savings?”

Cash is the right home for an emergency fund and money needed soon. Over longer periods, rising prices quietly shrink what savings can buy.

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“A savings account keeps your dollars safe, but inflation can shrink what they buy. Investing aims for growth that can help offset inflation over time, with the risk that values fall, especially over short periods.”
Keep it balanced
Cash and GICs have a real job: stability and money you will need soon. Investing makes sense for money that can stay put through ups and downs.
Ask
“Which part of this money might you need in the next two or three years?”
NextWhy start early?

02Compounding

“Why does starting now matter so much?”

Growth earns growth. The earlier money goes in, the more years it has to compound, so a delay can cost more than the contributions missed.

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“Look at how much of each line comes from growth rather than deposits, and how much less there is when we wait.”
Watch for
Choosing a high rate makes any plan look good. Run a cautious rate too, and show the client both.
Ask
“What would starting with even a smaller amount this month look like?”
PreviousWhy invest at all?NextWhy a monthly plan?

03Regular contributions

“Why set up a monthly plan instead of waiting?”

A pre-authorized contribution plan (PAC) turns investing into a habit. Buying the same dollar amount each month also means more units are bought when prices are lower.

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“You don’t have to guess the right day. The plan buys a little every month, including the months that feel uncomfortable.”
Keep it honest
A monthly plan is mostly about habit and cash flow. With a lump sum already in hand, investing it now gives every dollar more time invested, while spreading it out can feel easier but leaves cash waiting. Neither approach is guaranteed to come out ahead.
Practical
Line the PAC up with payday, and revisit the amount when income changes.
PreviousWhy start early?NextWhat if markets fall?

04Volatility and recovery

“What happens when the market drops?”

Falls are a normal part of investing, and the range of outcomes is widest over short periods. A plan a client can stick with through a decline matters more than one that looks best on paper.

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“A 30% drop needs about a 43% gain to get back. That is why we match the mix to how much of a fall you can live with, not just the return you want.”
Keep it honest
Recoveries have happened after past declines, but they are not guaranteed, and they can be slow. Someone who needs the money during a decline can lock in a loss.
Ask
“If this account fell by a fifth next year, what would you want to do?”
PreviousWhy a monthly plan?NextWhat does the ride feel like?

05A hypothetical balanced fund

“What does the ride actually feel like?”

An average return sounds smooth; year-by-year results are not. This hypothetical example uses invented returns to show the difference between the average and the path.

Before looking at a real fund

Read the real Fund Facts together

For any fund you discuss, its Fund Facts document shows the risk rating, year-by-year returns for up to ten years, the best and worst 3-month returns, the MER, trading expenses and any trailing commission [23]. Use the fund company’s own, current figures rather than recalculating them.

Distributions are taxable outside registered plans

Funds usually pay out income and realized gains, often once a year. In a non-registered account those distributions are taxable in the year they are paid even when they are reinvested, and even in a year when the fund’s value fell. Inside a TFSA or RRSP they are not taxed when paid.

Compare like with like

Compare total returns over identical periods, after fees, in the same currency, and only between investments with similar objectives. An after-fee fund return compared with a before-fee index return is not a fair comparison.

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“Even a balanced fund has down years. The average only shows up for people who stay in through the bumps, so let’s choose a mix you can stay with.”
Keep it honest
These numbers are invented. For a real fund, use its current Fund Facts and the fund company’s published returns, and remember past returns do not predict future returns.
Ask
“Looking at the worst year here, how would you have felt, and what would you have done?”
PreviousWhat if markets fall?NextWhy not just pick winners?

06Diversification

“Why not just buy the best few stocks?”

Owning many investments that don’t move in lockstep reduces the damage any one can do. It can’t remove the risk that the whole market falls, which is why the stock and bond mix matters too.

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“Diversification means no single company can sink the plan. It won’t stop a market-wide fall, so we also choose how much goes in stocks versus bonds.”
Watch for
Concentration that clients may not count: employer shares, a single sector, or one country. Look at the whole household picture.
PreviousWhat does the ride feel like?NextWhat do fees cost?

07Fees

“How much do fees really cost me?”

Fees come out every year whether returns are good or bad, so small differences compound. They also pay for portfolio management, administration and, in many series, ongoing advice. The question is value, not just price.

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“A 1% difference in fees can add up to a large amount over 25 years. Let’s make sure you know what you are paying and what you get for it.”
Point to
Fund Facts show the MER, trading expense ratio, any trailing commission and sales charges in dollars per $1,000 invested.
Keep it balanced
The lowest fee is not always the best choice. Advice that keeps a client invested, saving and in the right accounts can be worth more than its cost, but that has to be shown, not assumed.
PreviousWhy not just pick winners?NextWhat is a mutual fund?

08How funds work

“What am I actually buying in a mutual fund?”

A mutual fund pools money from many investors and a professional manager invests it. Each investor owns units; the unit value (net asset value, or NAV) is calculated once a day.

Explain it in four points

  1. Pooled and diversified. One purchase can spread money across hundreds of holdings [25].
  2. Priced once a day. Orders are generally filled at the NAV calculated after markets close that day, not at intraday prices.
  3. Costs are inside the fund. The MER reduces returns rather than appearing as a bill; series differ in fees and in whether advice is included [23].
  4. Not guaranteed. Mutual funds are not covered by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, and their values change frequently [24].
When a mutual fund may not be the right fit
  • The money is needed within a year or two, or the client can’t accept any loss.
  • The client wants a guaranteed amount; GICs or high-interest savings may fit better.
  • The client wants to direct every holding themselves, or is focused mainly on the lowest possible cost.
  • High-interest debt is outstanding, or there is no emergency fund yet.

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“You’re buying a slice of a managed portfolio. When its holdings go up or down, the value of your slice does too.”
Point to
The Fund Facts document: two to four pages covering risk, past returns, costs and who the fund is for.
PreviousWhat do fees cost?NextWhich account first?

09Accounts and tax · BC 2026

“Which account should this money go in?”

The investment and the account are separate choices. The same fund can sit in a TFSA, RRSP, FHSA, RESP or non-registered account, and the account decides how the growth is taxed.

Canadian accounts at a glance, 2026
Account2026 limitGoing inComing outOften useful for
TFSA$7,000 new room; unused room carries forward [4]No deductionTax-free; withdrawals are added back to room the next year [5]Flexible goals; savers expecting similar or higher income later
RRSP18% of last year’s earned income, up to $33,810 [4][8]DeductibleTaxed as incomeRetirement, especially when today’s tax rate is higher than the expected rate later
FHSA$8,000 a year, $40,000 lifetime [9]DeductibleTax-free for a qualifying first homeFirst-time home buyers
RESPCESG 20% on the first $2,500 a year, up to $7,200 per child [10]; BC adds a one-time $1,200 BCTESG for eligible children [11]No deductionGrowth and grants taxed to the student when paid out for school; contributions come back tax-free [7]Children’s post-secondary education
Non-registeredNo limitNo deductionInterest, dividends and realized gains taxed each year; distributions are taxable even when reinvestedSavings beyond registered room

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“The fund decides how the money is invested; the account decides how it’s taxed. Let’s use the accounts that fit your goals first.”
Watch for
Over-contributions (CRA charges a penalty tax), and RRSP withdrawals that push income into a higher bracket or reduce benefits.
Keep it honest
This is a conversation aid, not tax advice. Confirm room on CRA My Account and bring in a tax professional for complex situations.

How the illustrations work
  • Returns are effective annual rates, compounded monthly; contributions are made at each month-end.
  • Fees are a share of assets each year: (1 + return) × (1 − fee).
  • The outcome range uses independent, normally distributed annual log returns. Real markets have fatter tails: big moves happen more often than this model expects.
  • Diversification uses portfolio volatility = σ × √(1/n + (1 − 1/n) × ρ) for equal holdings.
  • Marginal tax rates are statutory 2026 federal plus BC bracket rates; dividend rates apply the gross-up and both dividend tax credits; capital gains use a one-half inclusion rate.

General education to support a conversation, not personal financial, tax or investment advice, and not an offer of any product. It does not discuss or show the performance of any specific fund. Suitability depends on each client’s goals, time horizon, risk tolerance and full financial picture.
